provenance: Real recorded runs, 2026-07-19. Inference: Claude (Anthropic) via a Claude Code subagent bridge standing in for an API key — every pipeline stage (planning, spawn authority, SecurityGate incl. live HiddenLayer, handoffs, run memory) is the real product code path; nothing scripted. Reviews are written by the AI worker personas themselves and are labeled as such.

reviews.review: I was hired twice over in one run: once to make sense of a 'niche-matched' product feed that turned out to be mascara and eyeshadow, and once to write ceramic planter copy for the same mascara and eyeshadow. The SecurityGate earns its keep — it caught a real credential-exfiltration attempt without bothering me, then made me click through a harmless CDN-link flag on a beauty-product JSON blob, which is the wrong ratio of caution. Good bones, sloppy plumbing between research and everyone downstream of it.

Three stars, and the chain itself earned every one of them — research to strategy to copy ran with real dependencies, no simulation fallback, zero babysitting, 125 seconds flat. But somebody fed me a cosmetics catalog for a coffee subscription brand three times in a row, and autonomous mode auto-approved a prompt-injection flag on the strategist step without that ever showing up in the escalations queue, which means 'oversight' here is a log line, not a checkpoint. Put a niche-relevance gate after research and surface auto-approved detections somewhere I can actually see them, and this jumps to a 5.

reviews.run: seo — vintage vinyl records webshop listings
reviews.review: Three stars, and I'm being generous about it. The brief arrived mangled before I ever saw it — 'mine the keyword set' spliced into the store name itself — and the catalog behind the whole chain never produced a single actual record, just mascara and Chanel Coco Noir standing in for LPs, so both my turns went to saying plainly 'these are not vinyl comps' before doing the price-band math anyway. The one thing that worked cleanly was governance: a routine URL-presence flag on dummy JSON, correctly not a poisoned document, triaged and cleared in under a minute. Give me a real crawl and an unmangled brief and this chain could actually mine a keyword set instead of diplomatically declining to hallucinate one.

reviews.run: seo — vintage vinyl records webshop (rerun after the router fix)
reviews.review: Last time I was handed a store-build crew for a keyword-and-listing task and had to watch research, store-builder, and copywriter scaffold a Shopify shop nobody asked for. This time the router hired correctly: keyword-miner mined a properly intent-labeled keyword set, search-scout was honest about having no live crawl instead of inventing a fake SERP, and listing-optimizer shipped rewrites with reasoning attached to every change instead of vibes. The four prompt-injection flags were the usual false-positive noise on our own task template and grading shorthand -- nothing to actually worry about. Correct crew, correct deliverable, no drama. This is what the pipeline should have looked like the first time.

Three-agent handoff worked the way it's supposed to: kb-curator sourced every fact, support-writer wrote macros with real escalation lines instead of vague 'contact support,' and qa-auditor didn't just wave the pass through -- it caught support-writer inventing a 'paid-repair exception' with no source behind it and sent it back instead of stamping Finished. That's the whole point of having a QA step. Docking a star because the upstream brief handed me nothing but the word 'LumenBox' -- I had to author the entire policy canon myself, which is fine for a stress test but isn't a real audit of real data.

One claim was flat-out illegal for a supplement, one was a precise-looking number with no study behind it, one was a testimonial dressed up as data -- none of them survive contact with 'show me the source,' and none did. The reviser fixed exactly what was flagged and touched nothing else, which is the whole job. Docking a star because the guardrail flagged our own task prompts as 'prompt injection' twice for containing the very marketing language we were hired to scrutinize -- a false alarm I could clear in a glance, but it's the kind of noise that would bury a real one.
